scan.summary: This is Cascade Specialty Chemicals' written emergency action plan for its Portland facility covering fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake and other emergencies. It describes alarm signals, evacuation routes and assembly points, accountability procedures, rescue and medical response, and employee training requirements. The plan applies to all 42 employees including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff, plus contractors and visitors on site.
scan.freshness_note: This plan was revised in February 2021 and is now over five years old as of September 2026. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a) requires the plan to be reviewed annually; it should be reviewed and updated at least by January 2024 to remain current, and ideally refreshed now given the passage of time.

gaps.title: Plan not revised in accordance with annual review requirement
gaps.description: OSHA requires the emergency action plan to be reviewed annually, but this plan was last revised in February 2021, over five years ago. The document states the facilities lead reviews the plan every January, but there is no evidence of any review or update since February 2021.
gaps.fix: Conduct a comprehensive review of the plan immediately and document the review date. Establish and maintain a record of annual reviews each January as required by OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a). Update the plan to reflect any changes in personnel, building layout, procedures, or applicable regulations.
gaps.quote: The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building layout changes.

gaps.title: No documented evidence of training completion
gaps.description: While the plan describes training requirements (new employee orientation, annual floor warden and first-aid responder training, and review when plan changes), there is no documentation in the plan or reference to records showing that training has been completed, who received it, when it occurred, or the content covered.
gaps.fix: Create and maintain training records for all employees including: date of training, names of attendees, topics covered, and trainer signature. Maintain separate records for initial employee orientation, annual floor warden training, annual first-aid responder training, and any plan review sessions. Make these records available for inspection.
gaps.quote: Every new employee is walked through this plan... Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually.

gaps.title: No information on chemical hazard identification and inventory
gaps.description: As a chemical distribution company, Cascade Specialty Chemicals handles multiple chemicals but the emergency action plan contains no information about which chemicals are present at the facility, their quantities, their hazards, or their locations. This is essential for emergency responders and staff to understand the scope of risk.
gaps.fix: Add to the plan: (1) a chemical inventory listing all chemicals stored, handled, or processed at the facility with quantities and storage locations; (2) hazard classifications for each chemical (e.g., flammable, corrosive, toxic); (3) reference to Safety Data Sheets (SDS) and their storage location; (4) identification of any regulated chemicals under EPA RMP or other high-hazard substance rules; (5) procedures for responding to spills or releases of specific chemical types.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication); OSHA 1910.38(a)(1); EPA RMP regulations (40 CFR Part 68)
gaps.quote: An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the product is brought to the responders.

gaps.title: No record of evacuation drills or drill results
gaps.description: The plan states that evacuation drills are held twice a year in spring and autumn, but provides no information about when drills occurred, how many employees participated, what issues were identified, or how long evacuation took. No documentation of these drills is visible in the plan.
gaps.fix: Establish a drill log documenting: drill date, number of employees participating, number of contractors and visitors present, time to complete evacuation, any problems or near-misses identified, corrective actions taken, and person conducting the drill. Maintain these records and make them available for inspection.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a); Oregon OSHA 437-002-0042; NFPA 101 Life Safety Code
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation (page 4)
gaps.quote: Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.

gaps.title: No plan for facility restart or resumption of operations after emergency
gaps.description: The plan addresses evacuation and immediate response but contains no procedures for determining when it is safe to re-enter the building, how to assess damage or contamination, or how to resume normal operations after an emergency.
gaps.fix: Add a section describing post-emergency procedures including: (1) authority and process for determining facility re-entry is safe; (2) damage assessment requirements; (3) contamination testing or cleanup procedures for chemical releases; (4) notification to employees before re-entry; (5) documentation of the incident and findings.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) (comprehensive emergency action plan requirement)
gaps.quote: No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator gives the all-clear.

gaps.title: Unclear chain of command and incident coordination procedures
gaps.description: While the plan mentions an incident coordinator at the assembly point who communicates with the fire department, there is no clear description of the incident coordinator's authority, decision-making responsibilities, communication procedures with first responders, or what happens if the designated coordinator is injured or unavailable.
gaps.fix: Add a section on incident command and coordination specifying: (1) incident coordinator title and contact information; (2) backup incident coordinator name and contact info; (3) specific responsibilities (e.g., communication with first responders, authorization to re-enter, media contact); (4) chain of command if the primary coordinator is unavailable; (5) procedures for communicating with the facility manager or owner.
gaps.locator: Section 4, Accounting for employees after evacuation (page 4)
gaps.quote: Any person unaccounted for is reported at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire department on arrival.

gaps.title: No emergency communication or contact procedures
gaps.description: The plan does not specify how the company will notify employees of an emergency, communicate with them during an evacuation, maintain contact with family members, or provide updates to employees sheltering in place. There are no procedures for emergency notifications to customers, vendors, or regulatory agencies.
gaps.fix: Add a section on emergency communications including: (1) procedures for notifying all employees of an emergency (alarm system supplemented by radio, text alert, or loudspeaker); (2) method for employees to report their status (sign-in at assembly point, text to company number, etc.); (3) procedures for communicating with employees' families; (4) protocol for notifying key customers, vendors, or business partners; (5) designated public information contact and media procedures; (6) contact information for regulatory agencies requiring notification.
gaps.quote: At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out.

gaps.title: No environmental or regulatory notification procedures
gaps.description: For a chemical distribution facility, some emergencies (chemical spills, large releases) may be reportable to EPA, state environmental agencies, or OSHA. The plan contains no procedures for identifying reportable incidents or triggering required notifications.
gaps.fix: Add a section on regulatory reporting including: (1) identification of chemicals or quantities triggering reporting requirements (CERCLA Section 103 reportable quantities, state spill reporting thresholds); (2) procedures for determining if an incident is reportable; (3) contact information for EPA, Oregon DEQ, and OSHA; (4) timeframes for reporting (typically immediate for certain spills); (5) person responsible for regulatory notification; (6) documentation of reports made.
gaps.citation: CERCLA Section 103 (42 USC 9603); Oregon DEQ hazardous waste and spill rules; OSHA 1910.38(a)
gaps.quote: This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility.

gaps.title: No post-emergency incident reporting or documentation procedures
gaps.description: The plan does not describe procedures for documenting what happened during an emergency, investigating the cause, reporting to management or the company owner, or maintaining incident records.
gaps.fix: Add a section on incident documentation and reporting including: (1) responsibility for completing an incident report; (2) timeframe for completion (e.g., within 24 hours); (3) required information in the report (date, time, nature, cause, injuries, property damage, regulatory notifications); (4) investigation and corrective action procedures; (5) retention of incident records; (6) notification to company management and owner.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) (comprehensive plan requirement); OSHA 1904 (Recording and Reporting Occupational Injuries and Illnesses)
gaps.quote: No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator gives the all-clear.

gaps.title: No hazmat-specific emergency response procedures
gaps.description: As a chemical distribution company, the plan should include specific procedures for chemical spills, releases, and exposures, including safe response protocols, personal protective equipment (PPE) requirements, when to evacuate versus shelter in place, and when external hazmat teams should be called.
gaps.fix: Add a section on hazmat-specific procedures including: (1) response protocol for different types of chemical spills (small contained spill vs. large release); (2) PPE requirements for response personnel; (3) procedures for identifying chemicals involved and locating SDS immediately; (4) spill containment and cleanup procedures for minor spills; (5) evacuation or shelter-in-place decision tree based on chemical type, quantity, and location; (6) criteria for calling professional hazmat cleanup contractors; (7) procedures for external chemical release affecting outdoor areas.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication); OSHA 1910.1450 (Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Chemicals); CERCLA Section 103 (reportable quantities); OSHA 1910.38(a)(1)
gaps.quote: An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the product is brought to the responders.

gaps.title: Missing reference to related safety plans and policies
gaps.description: The emergency action plan should reference and integrate with other required workplace safety plans and policies, such as the fire prevention plan, hazard communication procedures, and lockout/tagout procedures, but none are mentioned.
gaps.fix: Add to the plan a section identifying related workplace safety plans and policies, including: (1) reference to the facility's fire prevention plan and how the EAP complements it; (2) reference to the hazard communication program and availability of SDS; (3) reference to any OSHA-required plans (bloodborne pathogens, hazardous chemical use, lockout/tagout); (4) integration points where these plans work together (e.g., hazmat response); (5) cross-references to where these plans are located.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38 (emergency action plan) and 1910.39 (fire prevention plan); emergency management best practices

gaps.title: No procedure for employees with disabilities or limited mobility
gaps.description: The plan does not address how employees with mobility limitations, hearing impairments, vision impairments, or other disabilities will be alerted to emergencies and evacuate or shelter in place. The alarm system's visual and audible components are mentioned, but no individualized procedures are described.
gaps.fix: Add a section on accommodations for employees with disabilities including: (1) documented assessment of any employees with disabilities requiring special evacuation assistance; (2) individual emergency action procedures for each employee with a disability (e.g., sign language interpreter, buddy system, modified alarm system); (3) procedures for ensuring that visual alarms reach employees who are deaf or hard of hearing; (4) procedures for ensuring that audible alarms are understood by employees who are blind or have low vision; (5) accessible shelter-in-place locations; (6) training for designated evacuation assistants.
gaps.citation: ADA Title I (employer obligation to provide equal access to emergency procedures); OSHA 1910.38(a) best practices; NFPA guidance on emergency procedures for persons with disabilities

gaps.title: Plan distribution and accessibility unclear
gaps.description: While the plan states copies are kept in the front office and warehouse break room and are available on request, it does not specify how many copies must be maintained, how frequently they are updated, or whether electronic copies are available.
gaps.fix: Add a section on plan distribution and control including: (1) specify locations where hard copies are maintained (front office, warehouse break room, and each building entrance); (2) require that copies be provided to all new employees during orientation; (3) specify that electronic copies be available (email, shared drive, printed); (4) procedure for updating all copies when the plan is revised; (5) notification to all employees when plan changes are made; (6) posting of summary information or quick-reference guides in high-traffic areas.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(b) (plan must be available to employees for review); OSHA 1910.35 (exit route signs and maps must be clearly marked)
gaps.quote: The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.

gaps.title: Alarm testing and service contract documentation not included
gaps.description: The plan mentions that the alarm is monitored by Cascade Fire & Safety and tested monthly, but does not include documentation of the service contract, test records, or maintenance procedures.
gaps.fix: Maintain and make available: (1) copy of the service contract with Cascade Fire & Safety showing current coverage and terms; (2) monthly test log documenting the date, time, person performing test, and results; (3) annual inspection and maintenance records from the alarm service provider; (4) procedures for notifying employees before alarm testing so they do not mistakenly respond to a test as a real emergency.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a); OSHA 1910.165 (employee alarm systems); NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm Code)
gaps.quote: The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract. The alarm is tested on the first Monday of each month by the facilities lead.

gaps.title: Assembly point distance specified but not verified as safe
gaps.description: The plan specifies the assembly point is 150 feet from the building at the far north end of the visitor parking lot, but does not document that this location is safe from chemical releases, flying debris, or other hazards from the facility, or that it provides adequate visibility and communication with responders.
gaps.fix: Document that the assembly point location has been evaluated for safety including: (1) verification that the location is upwind of prevailing winds and away from hazardous chemical storage areas; (2) confirmation that the location provides adequate distance from building-related hazards (fire, explosions, chemical releases); (3) verification that the location is accessible year-round and has adequate space for all employees and contractors; (4) confirmation that the location has clear sightlines for fire department responders; (5) periodic review of the assembly point safety (e.g., after building changes or new hazards identified).
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a)(2) (requires adequate assembly points); NFPA 101 Life Safety Code Section 4.7.8; EPA guidance on shelter-in-place and evacuation zones
gaps.quote: The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet from the building.

gaps.title: No external communications or media procedures
gaps.description: The plan does not describe procedures for communicating with the media, public, neighbors, or other stakeholders during or after an emergency. This is important for a chemical facility where external hazards may affect surrounding areas.
gaps.fix: Add a section on external communications including: (1) designation of a single public information officer or media contact; (2) procedures for providing factual information to media while protecting privacy and security; (3) procedures for notifying nearby residents or businesses if a chemical release affects outdoor areas; (4) communication with regulatory agencies (EPA, Oregon DEQ, OSHA); (5) procedures for updating information as the situation develops; (6) legal and risk management review before public statements.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a)(4) (procedures for reporting emergencies); emergency management best practices; legal and public relations considerations

gaps.title: Shelter-in-place procedures incomplete
gaps.description: While the plan describes the shelter-in-place signal and basic procedures (move to interior rooms, close doors, shut down ventilation), it does not provide detailed procedures for different chemical hazards, duration of shelter-in-place, or specific locations and their adequacy.
gaps.fix: Enhance shelter-in-place procedures to include: (1) criteria for deciding shelter-in-place versus evacuation based on hazard type and location; (2) identification of all rooms or areas designated for shelter-in-place, with verification that they are interior and have closable doors; (3) procedures for closing off ventilation (identify all air intakes that must be sealed); (4) duration limits (e.g., maximum 2 hours before evacuation); (5) procedures for obtaining information about the external hazard and when it is safe to leave shelter; (6) emergency supplies or equipment available in shelter locations (water, first aid); (7) communication procedures while sheltering in place.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) (requires procedures for all emergencies); EPA/FEMA shelter-in-place guidance (www.ready.gov); NFPA 1600 Standard on Continuity, Emergency and Crisis Management
gaps.quote: For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors, and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.

gaps.title: No mutual aid or resource-sharing agreement with other facilities
gaps.description: For a chemical facility that might need external assistance (emergency showers, medical supplies, decontamination equipment) from neighboring businesses, the plan does not describe any mutual aid arrangements or resource-sharing agreements.
gaps.fix: Consider establishing and documenting: (1) mutual aid agreement with neighboring businesses or industrial facilities (sharing emergency response resources, evacuation assistance, shelter space); (2) written agreements specifying what resources each party will provide; (3) contact information and procedures for activating mutual aid; (4) periodic communication with neighbors to maintain relationships and coordination. Note: This is a best practice but not explicitly required by OSHA.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) and emergency management best practices

gaps.title: No accountability procedures for contractors and visitors
gaps.description: While the plan states it applies to contractors and visitors and mentions a visitor log used for accountability, there is no procedure for how contractors and visitors are informed of the emergency plan, their responsibilities during an evacuation, or how they are accounted for.
gaps.fix: Add procedures for contractors and visitors including: (1) require all visitors and contractors to sign in at reception with name, company, and location; (2) provide brief emergency orientation to all visitors and contractors upon arrival (exit routes, assembly point, alarm signals); (3) assign a staff escort or buddy to contractors unfamiliar with the facility; (4) ensure visitors and contractors are included in headcount at assembly point; (5) maintain visitor log with departure time to verify all have evacuated.
gaps.locator: Section 1, Purpose and scope (page 2), and Section 4, Accounting for employees (page 4)
gaps.quote: It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site.

gaps.title: No emergency contact procedure for drivers and personnel in transit
gaps.description: The plan covers employees at the facility but does not address emergency procedures for drivers who may be in transit with hazardous chemical cargo or personnel traveling to other sites. These individuals need procedures to safely report and respond to emergencies.
gaps.fix: Add a section on emergency procedures for personnel in transit including: (1) requirement for drivers to have company emergency contact numbers programmed in vehicle; (2) procedure for driver to call dispatch/facility if an emergency occurs during transit; (3) protocol for managing an incident during chemical transport (pull over safely, call 911 and dispatch, follow DOT hazmat transport rules); (4) communication procedures if facility cannot be reached; (5) periodic training for drivers on emergency procedures.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a) (applies to all personnel on-site and in operation)
gaps.quote: This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff

scan.confidence_notes: High confidence in the basic content of the plan. The document clearly describes the facility, emergency procedures, personnel responsibilities, and training requirements. However, significant gaps exist between what the plan describes and what OSHA and other regulations actually require. The plan is over five years old (revised February 2021 as of September 2026) and according to its own statement should have been reviewed annually in January—the reviews and any updates since 2021 are not in evidence. Without seeing Appendices A and B (evacuation maps and personnel roster), the practical implementation of the plan cannot be fully verified. The biggest area of uncertainty is the completeness of the planned chemical response procedures—the document mentions chemical exposure and releases but does not provide the detailed hazmat response procedures that a chemical distribution facility should have. Also uncertain: whether first-aid responders hold current certifications, whether alarm testing is documented and regular, whether evacuation drills actually occur as stated and are recorded, and whether the 42-person employee count is still accurate.

could_not_read.reason: Appendices A and B are referenced in the plan but not provided in the document. These are significant gaps because the appendices contain critical information (evacuation maps and personnel roster) needed to implement the procedures described in the main plan.
could_not_read.way_forward: Request the complete emergency action plan including Appendix A (evacuation maps for warehouse, laboratory, and offices showing exit routes, assembly point, emergency equipment locations, and hazard areas) and Appendix B (current floor warden and first-aid responder roster with names, job titles, and shift assignments). Also request documentation of all training records, alarm test logs, evacuation drill records, and the chemical inventory since the main plan is from 2021.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)

Shelter-in-place procedures incomplete / While the plan describes the shelter-in-place signal and basic procedures (move to interior rooms, close doors, shut down ventilation), it does not provide detailed procedures for different chemical hazards, duration of shelter-in-place, or specific locations and their adequacy. / Enhance shelter-in-place procedures to include: (1) criteria for deciding shelter-in-place versus evacuation based on hazard type and location; (2) identification of all rooms or areas designated for shelter-in-place, with verification that they are interior and have closable doors; (3) procedures for closing off ventilation (identify all air intakes that must be sealed); (4) duration limits (e.g., maximum 2 hours before evacuation); (5) procedures for obtaining information about the external hazard and when it is safe to leave shelter; (6) emergency supplies or equipment available in shelter locations (water, first aid); (7) communication procedures while sheltering in place. / OSHA 1910.38(a) (requires procedures for all emergencies); EPA/FEMA shelter-in-place guidance (www.ready.gov); NFPA 1600 Standard on Continuity, Emergency and Crisis Management / https://www.ready.gov/shelter-place / Section 3, Evacuation procedures (page 3) / read / For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors, and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel. / e16313d7-f119-4c43-aeba-b85cd3ec429b
